readings: Combinations (order does not matter, as with itertools.combinations), so each subset of a given length is counted once.
Permutations (order matters, as with itertools.permutations), so each ordering of a subset is counted separately. This adds more product terms and changes the result.

ambiguities.span: computes the logarithm of the products summed together
readings: 'summed together' attaches to 'the logarithm': take the logarithm of each product, then sum those logarithms.
'summed together' attaches to 'the products': first sum all the products, then take a single logarithm of that total.

judge.feedback: Both ambiguities are present and divergent. For ([2, 3],), the combinations reading gives log(2)+log(3)+log(6)=log(36). The permutations reading counts 6 twice and gives log(216). Summing the products first instead gives log(11). Two risks to intent: in combinatorics 'arrangements' usually means ordered selections (permutations), and 'the logarithm of the products summed together' most naturally parses as log(sum of products). Either could push the original reading below plausible. To keep the original reading competitive: (1) use a more neutral word such as 'groupings' or 'selections' instead of 'arrangements'; (2) phrase it so the attachment is genuinely balanced, e.g. 'It then computes the logarithm of each product and the results are summed', or 'computes the logarithms of the products, summed together'.
